name: Valuing Illiquid Tokens
title: Valuing Illiquid Tokens
answer: Valuing illiquid tokens covers digital assets that do not trade on an active market with reliable volume. This includes locked or vesting tokens, tokens with transfer restrictions, low-liquidity pairs, and pre-launch or delisted assets. The goal is to produce a fair value or carrying amount for financial statements, tax filings, or internal reporting. The work sits within digital asset accounting and overlaps with valuation, treasury, and audit functions.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Valuing illiquid tokens covers digital assets that do not trade on an active market with reliable volume. This includes locked or vesting tokens, tokens with transfer restrictions, low-liquidity pairs, and pre-launch or delisted assets. The goal is to produce a fair value or carrying amount for financial statements, tax filings, or internal reporting. The work sits within digital asset accounting and overlaps with valuation, treasury, and audit functions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on blockchain data sources, including full nodes, indexers, and explorers that record token balances, transfers, and smart contract terms. Market data aggregators and exchange APIs supply whatever thin trading data exists, while internal ledgers and accounting subledgers hold cost basis and transaction history. Valuation models are typically run in spreadsheets or specialized pricing engines that pull from these sources. Secure key management and custody records are part of the infrastructure because ownership and control affect value.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners usually begin with the last observable trade or a reference price from a comparable liquid token. They then adjust for illiquidity using a discount, a lock-up model, or an option pricing framework that accounts for time-based vesting. For tokens with no market at all, income or cost approaches may be used, such as discounting expected cash flows or referencing the cost to create or acquire the asset. The chosen method depends on the token's rights, the length of any restriction, and the availability of comparable data. Documentation of assumptions is a core part of the work.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on what the token actually grants, such as governance votes, fee shares, redemption rights, or access to a network, and whether those rights are enforceable. Provenance matters because a token's history, including lock-up terms, transfer restrictions, and prior ownership, can change its value and its regulatory treatment. Valuation uncertainty is high, and thin markets can be manipulated, so firms need internal controls, independent review, and clear audit trails. Custody and key management failures are a separate risk that can impair or destroy value. Accounting policies typically document how illiquidity and restrictions are measured and disclosed.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more standardized fair value frameworks for illiquid digital assets, driven by audit pressure and regulatory attention. Automated valuation models are likely to incorporate more on-chain data, such as liquidity pool depth and vesting schedules, in real time. Tokenization of traditional assets may bring more reference prices and reduce some illiquidity, while new types of restricted tokens will keep the problem alive. Accounting systems are moving toward continuous valuation with auditable data feeds and model governance.
